title: Porsche Debuts Modern Infotainment for Older Models—But Do I Want One?

body_markdown:
Ah, the late 2000s. Digital nannies hadn’t fully taken over our cars, and we all still thought automotive batteries were just the 12-volt units you could buy at AutoZone. But screens *had* started infiltrating our dashboards—first as small digital displays and later with double-DIN touchscreen units with integrated controls for navigation and[music](https://www.hagerty.com/media/opinion/conelrad-the-apocalyptic-symbols-on-1953-63-car-radio-dials/) . The results were awkward at best.


More than a decade later, these early screens and their tech feel incredibly dated—and as they age and begin to get glitchy, they’re often worse than having no screen at all. There are aftermarket solutions, of course, though they almost always look tacked on. Knowing that owners of its models appreciate the look of factory equipment, Porsche recently rolled out a solution, to be available in early 2027, called Porsche Classic Communication Management Plus (PCCM Plus), which offers all the utility of a modern screen (along with wireless Apple CarPlay and Android Auto) with OEM fitment for 2009–16 Boxsters, Caymans, and 911s.


This isn’t the first time Porsche Classic has rolled out new tech for older vehicles. The single-DIN PCCM has long been available for 911s, from the first-generation F-model through the 993, along with the 959, 924, 944, 968, and 928. And a double-DIN PCCM Plus unit can be had for 996 and 997.1 911s, along with 986 Boxsters and 987 Boxsters and Caymans.


Porsche


On the latest PCCM Plus for the 2009–16 models, along with the all-important wireless integration with your Apple or Android device, you get integrated Bluetooth and WiFi, navigation, and the ability to sync to parking sensors and steering-wheel-mounted controls, if your car is so equipped. It effectively updates these models, which already had screens, to current, if not bleeding-edge, tech. What’s more, the all-important volume knob and several key buttons appear to be maintained.


Porsche hasn’t yet announced pricing for the latest PCCM Plus, but the double-DIN kits for earlier cars cost about $1500 without navigation, and $1725 with mapping capability. The single-DIN units for earlier cars run about the same, depending on the vendor.


That’s a lot of money. Is it worth it? That depends on what your preferences are. A quick perusal of Crutchfield, a well-known stereo retailer, shows 111 CarPlay-equipped touchscreen units for a 2010 Porsche 911, and they range from a thrifty $199 to a Stuttgart-matching $1500. Most of those units are touchscreen-only, though some do offer a knob and some physical buttons.


Your author’s less-than-attractive head unit.


[Eddy Eckart](https://www.hagerty.com/media/author/eeckarthagerty-com/)


Porsche’s announcement coincides with my own debate about whether I should add one of the 986-compatible PCCM Plus units to[my 986 Boxster](https://www.hagerty.com/media/our-garage/bringing-boxster-back-1-eyes-wide-open/) . That $1500 price tag is way more than I want to spend for a head unit that may not be as powerful as some of the aftermarket ones out there. That said, there’s no question a factory unit looks better than the dorky Pioneer piece that’s currently in there. My car is right on the cusp of vehicles that could look OK with a big screen, but I also like the fact that it’s one of the last of the old-school, screenless interiors. I might feel differently if I had a newer model with an aging screen; the integration with the rest of the car’s functions, wireless CarPlay, and, most importantly, those OEM buttons, would probably put me over the top despite the Porsche tax.
